title: GCD and LCM
body:
**GCD**, the greatest common divisor: the largest integer that divides both. `gcd(12, 18)`
is 6.
**LCM**, the least common multiple: the smallest integer both divide. `lcm(4, 6)` is 12.

They are the same fact from two sides, and this identity is how you get the second from the
first:

$$\gcd(a,b) \times \text{lcm}(a,b) = a \times b$$

So `lcm(a, b) == a / gcd(a, b) * b`. Divide before multiplying, or a large `a * b` overflows
the [[Integer]] before the division ever happens.

## Euclid's algorithm

Do not loop from `min(a,b)` downwards looking for a divisor. Use the fact that any divisor of
`a` and `b` also divides `a % b`, which shrinks the problem fast:

```c++
int gcd(int a, int b) {
	while (b != 0) {
		int r = a % b;
		a = b;
		b = r;
	}
	return a;
}
```

```
gcd(48, 18) -> gcd(18, 12) -> gcd(12, 6) -> gcd(6, 0) -> 6
```

It terminates because the remainder strictly decreases and cannot go below 0, which is the
[[Division Algorithm]]'s guarantee doing the work. The recursive version is one line,
`return b == 0 ? a : gcd(b, a % b)`, and is the standard first example when [[Recursion]]
turns up at the end of the course.

Euclid's algorithm is also the course's first genuinely *clever* algorithm: trial division is
$O(n)$ in the size of the number, this is logarithmic. Why that difference matters is
[[Time Complexity]] in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]. It is proved properly in [[DISCRETE MATH]],
and the extended version of it is what makes RSA key generation work in [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]].

The correctness argument, the termination proof, and the extended version that produces
$\gcd(a,b) = ax + by$ are in [[Euclidean Algorithm]] ([[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]]). That
extended form is the only general way to invert an element in [[Modular Arithmetic]], which is the
step RSA key generation actually needs.
